paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) described familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type 3 (FHH3) as an autosomal dominant disorder of extracellular calcium homeostasis that involves the parathyroids, kidneys, and bone. Like FHH1 and FHH2, it features lifelong elevation of serum calcium with inappropriately low urinary calcium excretion. FHH1 and FHH2 are usually associated with normal circulating PTH, but FHH3 is distinguished by increased serum PTH, hypophosphatemia, and osteomalacia. Howles et al. (2016) stated that type 3 is clinically the most severe of the 3 types of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia.

paragraphs.text: McMurtry et al. (1992) described a large kindred with familial benign hypercalcemia. After the proposita was identified, they surveyed 46 kindred members from 5 generations, aged 1.5 to 91 years, by biochemical testing and/or chart review, and found 19 to be affected. Serum immunoreactive PTH (iPTH) was measured in 3 separate immunoassays in 15 hypercalcemic subjects. In this group, iPTH became supranormal by about age 30 years and appeared to rise further after that. Radiographic changes suggestive of osteomalacia were present in 3 of 5 affected adults older than 40 years who were studied. Two hypercalcemic adults underwent iliac crest biopsy after tetracycline labeling. In one of them, a 51-year-old woman, the biopsy confirmed defective skeletal mineralization. The authors concluded that the disorder may not be totally benign and that osteomalacia, perhaps due to mild hypophosphatemia, can develop in adulthood.

paragraphs.text: Hannan et al. (2010) studied 34 informative members of the Oklahoma kindred, 19 of them affected, using 24 polymorphic loci (17 microsatellites and 7 SNPs). The peak 2-point lod score was 6.92 at theta = 0 with D19S606. Recombinants in 3 individuals refined the FBHH3 locus to a 4.1-Mb interval flanked centromerically by D19S112 and telomerically by rs245111. The syntenic region on mouse chromosome 7 contains 4 Casr-related sequences (Gprc2a-rs genes), but the authors found no human or primate homologs of these genes in the human 19q13 region. Comparative analysis showed that 2 conserved segments are inverted in man and that an 11.6-Mb mouse region containing 35 genes, including the 4 Gprc2a-rs genes, is absent from the human genome. The authors therefore concluded that FBHH3 cannot be attributed to abnormalities of these genes.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on an affected individual from each of 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds, from Oklahoma and from Northern Ireland. Within the 3.46-Mb FHH3 interval on 19q13.3, they found a single shared variant: a C-T transition in exon 2 of the AP2S1 gene, predicting an arg15-to-cys (R15C) substitution. Dideoxynucleotide sequencing confirmed the variant, and restriction endonuclease analysis showed that it cosegregated with the disorder in 32 affected and 23 unaffected members from 4 generations of the 2 kindreds. The authors then sequenced AP2S1 in 50 unrelated FHH patients in whom CASR mutations had been excluded. They found 11 heterozygous missense mutations, all affecting arg15: 4 R15C, 3 R15H, and 4 R15L. The authors considered Arg15 a likely mutational hotspot because 3 different mutations at this residue were found in 13 unrelated probands and the residue was significantly conserved in 5,400 human exomes (p less than 10(-10)). In HEK293 cells stably expressing CaSR, all 3 mutants raised the EC50 for extracellular calcium, indicating reduced sensitivity to extracellular calcium. The R15C mutant also reduced CaSR endocytosis.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) noted that Arg15 of AP2-sigma-2 is conserved in all orthologs and in all human AP sigma subunit paralogs. In the AP2 crystal structure, Arg15 forms key contacts with the glutamine at position -4 of cargo dileucine motifs. Modeling predicted that the Cys15 and Leu15 substitutions would reduce affinity for the dileucine motif; the effect of His15 was harder to predict. CaSR has a C-terminal dileucine motif (RHQPLL, residues 1009-1014). In HEK293 cells, replacing Leu-Leu1013-1014 with Ala-Ala raised the EC50 of CaSR (3.63 vs 3.41 mM for wildtype; p less than 0.0001), indicating that the motif is functionally significant. In HEK293 cells stably expressing CaSR, the R15C, R15H, and R15L mutants raised the EC50 for extracellular calcium to 2.90, 2.73, and 2.86 mM, respectively, compared with 2.53 mM for wildtype (all p less than 0.0001). Cells with the Cys15 mutant had an EC50 significantly higher than cells with vector alone, which the authors suggested indicates a possible dominant-negative effect. After stimulation with extracellular calcium, cells transfected with wildtype AP2S1 showed a greater reduction in cell-surface CaSR than cells transfected with the R15C mutant or with vector alone. The authors concluded that AP2-sigma-2 has a role in CaSR endocytosis and in CaSR signaling, and that disruption by Arg15 mutants results in FHH3. Because AP2-sigma-2 is ubiquitously expressed, they suggested that Arg15 has a specific role, such as recognizing the CaSR dileucine motif, which would explain why the mutations cause a specific disorder of calcium homeostasis rather than a multisystem disease.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on affected members of 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds, from Oklahoma and from Northern Ireland. Both carried a heterozygous C-T transition in exon 2 of the AP2S1 gene, resulting in an arg15-to-cys (R15C) substitution. The mutation cosegregated with the disorder in 32 affected and 23 unaffected members of the 2 kindreds. The authors also found the R15C mutation in 4 of 50 unrelated FHH patients in whom CASR mutations had been excluded. In HEK293 cells stably expressing CaSR, the mutant raised the EC50 for extracellular calcium to 2.90 mM, compared with 2.53 mM for wildtype. This EC50 was also significantly higher than with vector alone, suggesting a possible dominant-negative effect. The mutant also reduced calcium-stimulated CaSR endocytosis.
